title: As Israel looks toward elections, some voters see a defining moment
text:
As Israel looks toward elections, some voters see a defining moment
Israel’s elections on Tuesday will serve as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in the nation’s history. Special correspondent Ilan Ben Zion recently joined international desk editor Matthew Bell in Boston to talk about what’s at stake.
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, Oct. 27, for the country’s sixth national election since 2019. This vote is also the first opportunity for Israel’s electorate to choose a new parliament since the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023 – and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
A lot has happened in the last three years. The Iran war that began in late February with a surprise attack by the United States and Israel is not resolved. Much of the Gaza Strip and southern Lebanon is buried in rubble, which has fueled global criticism of the Israeli military’s conduct in these wars. Israel’s relationship with the U.S. is under strain. The Israeli-occupied West Bank has seen a spate of violent attacks by Jewish settlers against Palestinians.
In many ways, these elections will serve as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history. Mr. Netanyahu’s critics hope to hand him a clear defeat. But the Israeli opposition is far from unified, and polls show that neither they nor the prime minister is likely to win an absolute majority in Tuesday’s contest.
From Haifa, in northern Israel, The Christian Science Monitor’s special correspondent Ilan Ben Zion recently joined international desk editor Matthew Bell in Boston to talk about Israel’s elections.
